title: Visual Guide to SQL Joins
description: Understand the mathematical Venn diagrams and physical execution engines (Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join) behind SQL joins.

data.text: A **JOIN** combines columns from one or more tables based on related column values. Under the hood, PostgreSQL's query optimizer evaluates the size of both tables and available indexes to select one of three join algorithms: **Nested Loop Join**, **Hash Join**, or **Merge Join**.

rows: For every row in outer table, loops through inner table looking for matches.
When outer table is small and inner table has a fast index on join column.
Builds an in-memory hash table of smaller table, then scans larger table probing hash keys.
When joining medium to large unindexed tables where equality (`=`) is used.
Sorts both tables on join keys, then scans both tables in parallel merging matches.
When both tables are already sorted (e.g. via B-tree index) or join condition is large.

data.caption: Relational Join Types Overview
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Table A] --> Join{Join Condition}
    B[Table B] --> Join
    Join --> C[INNER: Only matching rows]
    Join --> D[LEFT: All from A + matched B]
    Join --> E[RIGHT: All from B + matched A]
    Join --> F[FULL: All rows from both]
    Join --> G[CROSS: Cartesian Product A x B]

data.text: The algorithm in the table above is chosen by the planner at run time, not written in the SQL. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows which join was actually used, how many rows each step produced, and how much data was read from cache versus disk. Reading these plans is the core skill behind every join performance question.

data.title: Inspect the chosen join strategy
data.content: Look for the join node name (Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join), the estimated versus actual rows, and the buffer counts.
data.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
    ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- Hash Join  (cost=1.20..2.40 rows=100 width=40) (actual time=0.05..0.09 rows=98 loops=1)
--   Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
--   Buffers: shared hit=7
-- Planning Time: 0.1 ms
-- Execution Time: 0.2 ms

data.title: Interview angle: joins are physical operations
data.text: A common interview question is 'how does the database execute a join?'. A strong answer names the three physical algorithms, explains when each wins (nested loop for small indexed outer sets, hash join for large unsorted inputs, merge join for pre-sorted inputs), and mentions how to verify the choice with EXPLAIN and indexes. Naming the algorithm is what separates a SQL user from a database engineer.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Joins combine tables based on matching predicate keys.
PostgreSQL chooses between Nested Loop, Hash Join, and Merge Join based on cost estimates.
Indexing foreign key columns enables fast Nested Loop and Merge joins.
